design_detail: Cross-sectional analysis of 17 WHO World Mental Health surveys (fieldwork 2001–2005; probability household samples, nationally representative in most countries, regional or urban-only in China, Colombia, Japan, Mexico and Nigeria; 85,088 respondents) using the WHO CIDI 3.0 with retrospective ages of first use of tobacco, alcohol, cannabis and other illicit drugs. Outputs: cumulative use by age 29 by country and age cohort; discrete-time survival models (person-years to 29) of initiating a later drug after an earlier one, by country and cohort, and pooled across countries with an interaction between earlier-drug use and its prevalence; the prevalence of three 'gateway violations'; and pooled discrete-time survival models of dependence onset with violations, number of drugs used, age of onset and early mental disorders as predictors.
can_establish: How the order of first use of tobacco or alcohol, cannabis and other illicit drugs, as recalled by adults in 17 countries in 2001–2005, varied across countries and birth cohorts; whether the association between using an earlier drug and starting a later one was stronger or weaker where the earlier drug was more common; and whether out-of-order initiation went with later dependence.
cannot_establish: Whether using one drug causes use of another: no individual-level common causes are modelled, the instrumental-variable logic (prevalence varying for reasons unrelated to individual risk) is assumed rather than tested, and country or cohort prevalence is an ecological variable confounded with culture, law, drug markets and survey methods; the true timing of first use (ages recalled, often decades later); or precise country estimates where use was rare (several rest on fewer than 20 people and many models did not converge).

sample.recruitment: General population: probability household samples of adults, nationally representative except China (Beijing and Shanghai), Colombia and Mexico (urban areas, about 73–75% of the population), Japan (four metropolitan areas) and Nigeria (21 of the 36 states, about 57% of the population); France sampled from telephone numbers and the Netherlands from postal registries. Face-to-face interviews by trained lay interviewers; all respondents completed Part I, and Part II (said to contain the substance-use assessment) went to everyone with a core disorder and about 25% of the others, weighted back to the population. Weighted average response rate 69.9%, from 45.9% (France) to 87.7% (Colombia) (2. Method › 2.1 Sample; Table 1).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults 18 and over in most countries (16+ New Zealand, 20+ Japan, 21+ Israel, 18–65 Colombia and Mexico) (Table 1). Survival analyses restricted to person-years up to age 29 for comparability across cohorts (2.3 Analysis methods). Table 1 also lists a Part II subsample aged 44 or under (39 or under in Nigeria, China and Ukraine) whose use in this paper is not explained.
sample.demographics: Four age cohorts at interview (18–29, 30–44, 45–59, 60+); the sex and age composition of each sample is not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview); non-response ranged from 12.3% to 54.1% by country.
sample.selection_effects: Response was below 60% in Belgium, France, Germany, Japan and the Netherlands; coverage was regional or urban in five countries; people outside private households are outside the sampling frame. Older cohorts' reports of use before 29 depend on survival to interview and on long recall. Countries where a drug was rare contribute very few people who used it, so their country-level estimates are fragile.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported ever use and age at first use, recalled at interview: tobacco (even a puff), alcohol (any drink), cannabis, cocaine, and other drugs from a reference list (heroin, opium, glue, LSD, peyote or any other); 'other illicit drugs' combine cocaine and these drugs and exclude prescription drugs. Age of first tobacco use was not assessed in Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain, Japan and New Zealand, where violations involving tobacco were defined by a different rule (2.2 Measures; 2.2.1). Background prevalence of each earlier drug (by country, and in the Results by country and cohort) is the moderator in the pooled models.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not used: exposure is any use. Age of onset of regular use was asked but not analysed (4.1 Limitations, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: The subject of the paper: the order of first use across drug classes. Dependence models include tobacco and alcohol use and the number of illicit drug classes used as a time-varying covariate.

comparison.controls: Survival models compare person-years after with person-years before first use of the earlier drug within each country; pooled models compare countries or cohorts with different prevalence; dependence models compare people who started in the usual order with those who did not.
comparison.matching: None. Country models control for person-year and sex; pooled interaction models for gender, age cohort and country; dependence models for sex, age cohort, early-onset internalizing and externalizing disorders, age at onset and years since onset of use, tobacco and alcohol use, number of illicit drugs, the violations and country (2.3 Analysis methods; Table 5).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Individual propensities (behavioural disinhibition, family history, conduct problems before first use), peer and family drug use and individual access to drugs are not in the initiation models (early mental disorders enter only the dependence models); the national or cohort-level factors behind prevalence (culture, religion, law, markets) are not measured, as the authors note.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable: the analysis concerns sequences of drug use.

outcomes.instruments: WHO Composite International Diagnostic Interview version 3.0, fully structured and lay-administered, for DSM-IV dependence (alcohol, nicotine, drugs) and early-onset internalizing and externalizing disorders, with retrospective ages of onset (2.2 Measures). Nicotine dependence was not assessed in ten countries and drug dependence in six (Table 5, notes 5 and 6).
outcomes.validity_norms: Clinical calibration of the CIDI 3.0 is cited (Kessler et al., 2004). The authors acknowledge recall error in ages of first use and possible cross-national differences in willingness to report, which they tried to reduce with piloting, community endorsement, non-directive probing and self-completion of sensitive questions by literate respondents (4.1 Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.operationalization: Initiation: first use of any amount of the later drug class by 29. Violations: (1) cannabis before both alcohol and tobacco; (2) other illicit drugs before both alcohol and tobacco; (3) other illicit drugs before cannabis; a less strict version (before either alcohol or tobacco) is in supplementary tables. Dependence onset: onset of the full DSM-IV syndrome (2.2.1; Table 5).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (α=0.05, two-tailed). 10 counts the outcome types (initiation of cannabis and of other illicit drugs, three violations, five dependence outcomes); across 17 countries, four cohorts and the pooled models the paper reports well over 400 estimates and tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: structured lay interviews; sensitive questions self-administered by literate respondents.

analysis.effect_sizes: Pooled interactions (discrete-time survival across countries, adjusted for gender, age cohort and country): alcohol or tobacco initiation × prevalence of alcohol or tobacco use, for later initiation of other illicit drugs, OR 32.7 (95% CI 8.3 to 129.0); cannabis initiation × cannabis prevalence, for later other illicit drug initiation, OR 0.3 (0.2 to 0.6); no significant interaction for alcohol or tobacco and later cannabis (no estimate printed). The scale of the prevalence variable is not stated. Country examples (Table 3): cannabis and later other illicit drugs, total, USA OR 137.1 (94.8 to 198.3), New Zealand 118.0 (83.3 to 167.2), Netherlands 62.5 (9.6 to 406.5); at ages 18–29, Netherlands 7.4 (1.8 to 30.4) against USA 107.1 (57.9 to 198.1) and Spain 160.1 (36.8 to 695.9). Proportion of people using other illicit drugs by 29 who had not used cannabis first (Table 4, total): Japan 83.2%, Nigeria 77.8%, South Africa 59.2%, Mexico 48.4%, Colombia 33.4%, New Zealand 12.7%, USA 11.4%. Dependence (Table 5, pooled): violations largely unrelated (for example cannabis before tobacco and alcohol, alcohol dependence OR 0.6, 0.3 to 1.0), except other illicit drugs before cannabis and alcohol dependence (1.6, 1.1 to 2.3); number of drug classes used strongly related (classes: cannabis, cocaine, prescription drugs, other drugs; drug dependence among people who used cannabis: 2 classes 6.1, 3 classes 15.4, 4 classes 35.7, against 1); later age of onset of use protective (ORs 0.2 to 0.7, unit not stated); each early internalizing disorder 1.3 to 1.7 and each early externalizing disorder 1.2 to 1.7.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Secondary analysis of survey data; no registration or analysis plan is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Country-level rates for two of the three violations, the less strict definition and supplementary dependence models are only in a supplement (a Word file, not read); chi-square statistics for Table 5 are 'available upon request'; many country cells are omitted because models did not converge.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Estimates for rare drugs rest on very few people (Table 4's n column, people with the violation: Japan 13 of 16 who used other illicit drugs, Nigeria 7 of 8, Belgium 9, Israel 5), and many odds ratios have intervals spanning two to four orders of magnitude (for example Israel 18–29, cannabis and later other illicit drugs, 3650.6, 209.0 to 63,756.4).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In nearly every country with enough people who used drugs, starting an earlier drug in the usual sequence was followed by much higher odds of starting a later one, but the strength of the association varied across countries and cohorts. In pooled models the association of cannabis with later other illicit drug use was weaker where cannabis was more common, while the association of alcohol or tobacco with later other illicit drug use was stronger where alcohol or tobacco were more common. Starting out of order was more common where the earlier drug was rare (Japan, Nigeria, from a handful of respondents). Out-of-order starts were largely unrelated to later dependence, while the number of drug classes used, an earlier start and early mental disorders were related to it.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the gateway pattern 'at least partially reflects unmeasured common causes rather than causal effects', and that preventing specific gateway drugs may not by itself greatly reduce later drug use; the Conclusions say violations are not associated with dependence. Gaps: (1) variation of an association with national prevalence fits common causes, but also differences in drug markets, laws and measurement between countries and a changing make-up of the people who use a drug as it becomes common; the instrumental-variable reasoning is assumed, not tested, as the Limitations concede; (2) the two significant interactions point in opposite directions, and only the cannabis one fits the deviance-marker reasoning of the Introduction (a rarer drug marking higher-risk people), yet the Discussion counts both as support for environmental influences without addressing the contrast; (3) the prevention implication rests on cross-sectional associations, with no analysis of a change in prevalence within a country over time; (4) the Japan and Nigeria proportions rest on 16 and 8 people who used other illicit drugs (13 and 7 of them with the violation); (5) 'not associated with dependence' overstates the pooled results, where one violation was associated with alcohol dependence (OR 1.6). The Conclusions themselves speak of suggestive evidence.

timeline.event: Kandel: stages of adolescent drug involvement, the sequence this paper tests across countries.

Weiss et al.: in hospitalised patients the association of cocaine use with mood disorder weakened as cocaine use became more common, the analogy on which this paper's prevalence logic rests (as described in the Introduction).
Morral, McCaffrey & Paddock: a common-factor model reproduces the gateway pattern (cited for the common-cause explanation).
Wells & McGee, New Zealand Mental Health Survey: violations uncommon, more common in recent cohorts and not associated with dependence (as cited); the survey is one of the 17 pooled here.
Degenhardt et al., US National Comorbidity Survey Replication: same findings (as cited); also one of the 17 surveys pooled here.
This study: 17 WHO World Mental Health surveys.
Vanyukov et al. cite this study's Japan figures against the gateway hypothesis, combining age groups (see that card).

replication.where_it_stands: The cross-national description that the order of first use varies with how common each drug is, cited in the round's reading list as showing that the order varies between countries. No independent replication of the prevalence-interaction finding is named in the reading list or in the paper (the earlier New Zealand and US analyses use two of the same surveys). Its causal reading is weak by design, and the reading list notes that no study separates causal, common-liability and availability explanations in one design. Later uses of its numbers should keep the small numbers behind the Japan and Nigeria figures.

funding.funder: Not reported: the author manuscript on PMC contains no acknowledgments, funding or role-of-funder statement (the published version was not read).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported in the author manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: 23 authors from the WMH survey consortium (National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, Sydney; Harvard Medical School; national institutes and universities in the participating countries); the first author's group also wrote the earlier US analysis it cites (Degenhardt et al., 2009).

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts in several countries recording first use of each drug as it happens, with individual measures of liability before any use and of local availability and price, analysed with explicit instruments (for example abrupt changes in tobacco taxes or in cannabis law and supply) to test whether shifts in use of an earlier drug change use of later drugs beyond what liability and opportunity predict.

domains.note: Initiation models control only person-year and sex (country models) or gender, cohort and country (pooled models); the individual propensities that form the competing explanation under test are not modelled, and the moderator (country or cohort prevalence) is ecological and confounded with culture, law, drug markets and survey methods.

Ages of first use recalled, up to decades later; how onsets in the same year were ordered is not stated; age of first tobacco use was not asked in eight countries, so violations involving tobacco were defined differently there; 'other illicit drugs' lump cocaine with heroin, inhalants and hallucinogens.
Probability household samples with response rates of 45.9% to 87.7% (below 60% in five countries), regional or urban coverage in four countries and Part II subsampling corrected by weights.

Key measures were not assessed in several countries (tobacco onset, nicotine dependence, drug dependence), many country cells are missing because models did not converge, and item non-response and its handling are not described.

Initiation of the later drug and dependence onset are also recalled; willingness to report illicit use differs across countries, as the authors acknowledge, which bears directly on cross-country comparisons.

Hundreds of estimates without correction; parts of the violation results and the sensitivity analyses are only in the supplement; the scale of the pooled interaction terms is not given; Table 5 test statistics are available only on request.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a test of whether using one drug causes use of another, the risk of bias is high: individual-level common causes are not addressed, the key moderator is ecological, and all timing is recalled. As a description of how the order of first use and its associations vary across countries and cohorts, the study is stronger: large probability samples with a common instrument and fieldwork procedures, though with variable response, regional coverage in some countries and very few people who used rare drugs. Cite it for the cross-national variation in the order of initiation and for the pooled associations with dependence as associations; not as evidence that the gateway pattern is non-causal.

key_findings.finding: Seventeen WHO World Mental Health surveys (seven developing and ten developed countries), 85,088 adults in total (2372 in the Netherlands to 12,992 in New Zealand), fieldwork 2001–2005, weighted average response rate 69.9% (45.9% France to 87.7% Colombia).

Use by age 29 varied widely: alcohol lowest in South Africa (40.6%), Lebanon (52.8%), Nigeria (55.6%) and Israel (55.7%); tobacco low in South Africa (32.4%) and Nigeria (16.1%); cannabis very low in Nigeria (2.8%), Japan (1.6%) and China (0.3%) against a cross-country median of 9.8% and about 40% in the USA (40.9%) and New Zealand (40.1%); in Japan other illicit drugs (2.4%) were more common than cannabis. Most countries showed higher use in younger cohorts.
key_findings.locator: 3. Results › 3.1 Cross-national and cohort differences in drug use, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: With few exceptions, using a drug earlier in the sequence predicted starting a later one by 29 (country odds ratios mostly between about 10 and several hundred), but the strength varied: for cannabis and later other illicit drugs at ages 18–29, OR 7.4 (1.8 to 30.4) in the Netherlands against 107.1 (57.9 to 198.1) in the USA and 160.1 (36.8 to 695.9) in Spain.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Cross-national and age cohort differences in associations…, 1st paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Pooled across countries, the association of cannabis initiation with later other illicit drug initiation was weaker where cannabis use was more common (interaction OR 0.3, 0.2 to 0.6), whereas the association of alcohol or tobacco initiation with later other illicit drug initiation was stronger where alcohol or tobacco use was more common (OR 32.7, 8.3 to 129.0); no significant interaction for alcohol or tobacco and later cannabis.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Cross-national and age cohort differences in associations…, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The scale of the prevalence variable is not given, so the size of the interaction odds ratios cannot be interpreted; covariates gender, age cohort and country.

key_findings.finding: Starting other illicit drugs before cannabis was most common where cannabis was rare (Japan 83.2%, Nigeria 77.8%) and uncommon where cannabis was common (USA 11.4%, New Zealand 12.7%); starting other illicit drugs before both alcohol and tobacco was reported for 52.5% in Japan and 51.8% in Nigeria against 0.6% in Germany, 0.2% in New Zealand and 0.0% in Ukraine; 16.3% of people in South Africa who used cannabis had used neither alcohol nor tobacco before it.
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Cross-national and cross-cohort differences in violations…, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 4
key_findings.note: The Japan and Nigeria proportions in Table 4 rest on 16 and 8 people who used other illicit drugs by 29 (Table 2), of whom 13 and 7 started them before cannabis (Table 4's n column); the violation rates involving alcohol and tobacco come from supplementary tables (not read), and in Japan, Germany and New Zealand age of first tobacco use was not asked, so those rates use a different definition.

key_findings.finding: In pooled models of dependence onset, violations of the sequence were largely unrelated to dependence on any drug (one exception: other illicit drugs before cannabis and alcohol dependence, OR 1.6, 1.1 to 2.3), whereas the number of drug classes used (drug dependence among people who used cannabis: 6.1, 15.4 and 35.7 for 2, 3 and 4 classes against 1), an earlier start (age of onset ORs 0.2 to 0.7) and early internalizing (1.3 to 1.7 per disorder) and externalizing disorders (1.2 to 1.7) were related.
key_findings.locator: 3.3 Cross-national and cross-cohort differences in violations…, 3rd paragraph; Table 5
key_findings.note: The 'number of illicit drugs used' counts prescription drugs as one of its four classes (cannabis, cocaine, prescription drugs, other drugs; Table 5, note 4), unlike 'other illicit drugs', which exclude prescription drugs; the 6.1, 15.4 and 35.7 therefore include prescription drug use as a class.

key_findings.finding: Women had lower odds than men of alcohol dependence among people who drank (OR 0.4, 0.3 to 0.5) and of drug dependence among people who used cannabis (0.7, 0.5 to 0.8), with no significant difference for nicotine (1.0), cocaine (0.9) or other illicit drug dependence (0.8, 0.6 to 1.0).
key_findings.note: General-population samples; ages of first use and of dependence onset were recalled at a single interview; adjusted for age cohort, early mental disorders, age of onset and years since onset, other substance use, number of drugs, violations and country. The paper does not discuss these sex differences. The odds are per person-year of dependence onset among people who had used each drug (discrete-time survival), pooled across countries, and the countries differ by outcome: tobacco dependence was not assessed in 10 of the 17 countries and drug dependence not in 6 (Table 5, notes 5 and 6).

key_findings.finding: The authors acknowledge that ages of first use are recalled with error (tending to rise with repeated assessment, though the order is reported to stay stable), that willingness to report may differ across countries, that country is a coarse unit, and that no instrumental variable was measured.

The authors conclude that the evidence is suggestive that initiation is not constant across contexts, that the sequence is not immutable, and that age of onset and degree of exposure to any drug, rather than the order, predict dependence.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the cumulative use of 'tobacco or alcohol' is lower than that of alcohol alone for the USA at 18–29 (96.0% vs 96.2%; n 1316 vs 1318) and Ukraine at 18–29 (99.4% vs 99.7%; n 297 vs 298), which is impossible for a union.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2 (United States and Ukraine, 18 to 29)
reporting_issues.consequence: Small; the 18–29 percentages are projected estimates, which may explain the percentages but not the counts. It suggests the combined rows were computed separately and should not be added up by hand.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 marks as significant an odds ratio of 1.0 with interval 1.0 to 1.0 (Belgium, 60 and over, cannabis and later other illicit drugs) and an odds ratio of 14.7 whose interval includes 1 (0.9 to 236.7; Belgium, 30–44, alcohol or tobacco and later other illicit drugs); in Table 4, New Zealand's age-association χ2 of 28.6 is not marked significant while smaller values elsewhere are.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 3 (Belgium rows); Table 4 (New Zealand row)
reporting_issues.consequence: The significance markers are not reliable cell by cell; degenerate estimates from sparse data are presented alongside the others.

reporting_issues.issue: The pooled interaction odds ratios (32.7 and 0.3) are given without the scale of the prevalence variable, and the Methods describe the moderator as prevalence within each country while the Results speak of countries/cohorts.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, 2.3 Analysis methods, 2nd paragraph; 3.2, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the direction of the interactions can be used; their size cannot be interpreted or compared.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say substance use was assessed in Part II, but Tables 2 to 4 use Part I samples for Colombia, Mexico, Israel, South Africa and New Zealand, and Table 1 lists no Part II sample for Israel or South Africa. Table 2 is headed n=54,068, while the samples its footnotes name sum to 54,307 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, 2.1 Sample, 2nd paragraph; Tables 1 and 2 (footnotes 1 and 2)
reporting_issues.consequence: Which respondents were asked about drug use in each country, and the exact analytic sample, cannot be reconstructed from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: The n column of Table 4 is not defined; its values look like the number of people with the violation rather than the denominator (Japan 13, against 16 who used other illicit drugs by 29 in Table 2), and the Japan estimate for ages 18–29 (77.3%) carries a standard error of 52.4 points.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline proportions for Japan (83.2%) and Nigeria (77.8%) rest on about 16 and 8 people who used other illicit drugs; they show that the order can differ, not its population rate.

reporting_issues.issue: The sensitivity definition is described as cannabis use 'before either alcohol or cannabis use', which should presumably read alcohol or tobacco, and Table 2's oldest cohort is headed '<= 60' while Table 3 and the Methods use 60 and over.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, 2.2.1 Order of onset and violations of the gateway progression, last paragraph; Table 2 header
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor labelling errors; the less strict definition is clear from the Limitations (no use of one or the other of alcohol and tobacco).

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion calls the number of early-onset mental disorders an important moderator of the risk of developing dependence, but Table 5 enters early internalizing and externalizing disorders only as predictors, with no interaction terms.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should call early-onset disorders predictors of dependence onset (associated with it), not moderators.

reporting_issues.issue: The note on sample design under Table 1 says that nine of the 15 surveys were based on nationally representative household samples, while the paper pools 17 countries and Table 1 marks 12 samples as nationally representative.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the note appears to describe a different set of surveys. Coverage should be taken from Table 1's rows (not nationally representative: China, Colombia, Japan, Mexico and Nigeria).
